title.zh: 卷二十七 列傳第十七 孔靖 孔琳之 殷景仁
title.en: Volume 27 Biographies 17: Kong Jing, Kong Linzhi, Yin Jingren
title.raw: 卷二十七 列傳第十七 孔靖 孔琳之 殷景仁 Volume 27 Biographies 17: Kong Jing, Kong Linzhi, Yin Jingren

sentences.zh: 列傳第十七

translations.literal: Biographies 17
translations.idiomatic: Biographies 17

sentences.zh: 孔靖孔琳之殷景仁

translations.literal: Kong Jing, Kong Linzhi, Yin Jingren
translations.idiomatic: Kong Jing, Kong Linzhi, Yin Jingren

sentences.zh: 季恭始察孝廉，累遷司徒左西掾，未拜，遭母憂。

translations.literal: At first Ji Gong was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt; he rose through posts to Left Western Aide of the Minister of Education, but before taking appointment suffered mourning for his mother.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Gong was first selected as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate and climbed the ranks to Left Western Aide under the Minister of Education; before he could assume the post, his mother died and he entered mourning.

sentences.zh: 隆安五年，被起為山陰令，不就。

translations.literal: In the fifth year of Long'an he was recalled to serve as magistrate of Shanyin but declined.
translations.idiomatic: In Long'an 5 the court summoned him to be magistrate of Shanyin; he refused.

sentences.zh: 宋武帝東征孫恩，屢至會稽，過季恭宅，季恭正晝臥，有神人衣服非常，謂曰：「起！

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu of Song marched east against Sun En, he repeatedly came to Kuaiji and passed Ji Gong's house; Ji Gong was napping at midday when an extraordinary spirit in strange garb said to him, 'Rise!
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yu's eastern campaigns against Sun En brought him repeatedly to Kuaiji, and each time he passed Ji Gong's home. Once, while Ji Gong napped at noon, a supernatural figure in outlandish dress appeared and said, 'Get up!

sentences.zh: 天子在門。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven is at the door.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor stands at your gate.

sentences.zh: 」既而失之，遽出，適見帝，延入結交，執手曰：「卿後當大貴，願以身為托。

translations.literal: Then it vanished; he rushed out and met the emperor just then; the emperor invited him in and they formed a bond, clasping hands as he said, 'You will surely rise to great honor one day—I wish to entrust myself to you.
translations.idiomatic: It vanished at once. Ji Gong bolted outside and ran straight into Liu Yu, who drew him in and took him as an ally, gripping his hand: 'Your fortune will be great. I ask you to rely on me as I rely on you.

sentences.zh: 」於是曲意禮接，贍給甚厚。

translations.literal: Thereupon he bent every courtesy to receive him and supplied him with great generosity.
translations.idiomatic: From then on Ji Gong went out of his way to honor Liu Yu and lavished support on him.

sentences.zh: 帝后討孫恩，時桓玄篡形已著，帝欲于山陰建義。

translations.literal: Afterward, when the emperor went to suppress Sun En, Huan Xuan's usurpation was already plain to see, and the emperor wished to raise the standard of revolt at Shanyin.
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Yu later marched against Sun En, Huan Xuan's seizure of power was already obvious, and Liu Yu meant to launch his uprising from Shanyin.

sentences.zh: 季恭以山陰路遠，且玄未居極位，不如待其篡後，於京口圖之，帝亦以為然。

translations.literal: Ji Gong held that Shanyin was too far, and since Xuan had not yet reached the supreme position, it would be better to wait until after his usurpation and plot at Jingkou; the emperor agreed.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Gong argued that Shanyin lay too remote and that Huan Xuan had not yet taken the throne—better to wait until the usurpation was done and strike from Jingkou. Liu Yu accepted the counsel.

sentences.zh: 時虞嘯父為會稽內史，季恭求為府司馬不得，乃出詣都。

translations.literal: At the time Yu Xiaofu was Intendant of Kuaiji; Ji Gong sought appointment as Staff Major of the prefecture but did not obtain it, and so went out to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Xiaofu was then Intendant of Kuaiji. Ji Gong tried for the post of prefectural staff major and failed, so he left for the capital.

sentences.zh: 及帝定桓玄，以季恭為會稽內史，使齎封板拜授，正與季恭遇。

translations.literal: When the emperor settled Huan Xuan, he made Ji Gong Intendant of Kuaiji and sent a bearer with sealed appointment tablets to invest him; he happened to meet Ji Gong on the way.
translations.idiomatic: After Liu Yu defeated Huan Xuan, he appointed Ji Gong Intendant of Kuaiji and dispatched a messenger with the sealed commission—and met Ji Gong along the route.

sentences.zh: 季恭便回舟夜還，至即叩扉入郡。

translations.literal: Ji Gong turned his boat back that same night; upon arriving he knocked on the gate and entered the commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Gong reversed course and sailed through the night; at dawn he hammered on the yamen gate and took up office.

sentences.zh: 嘯父本為桓玄所授，聞玄敗，開門請罪。

translations.literal: Xiaofu had originally been appointed by Huan Xuan; hearing of Xuan's defeat, he opened the gates and petitioned for punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Xiaofu, a Huan Xuan appointee, heard of the defeat and opened the city to surrender himself to judgment.

sentences.zh: 季恭慰勉，使且安所住，明日乃移。

translations.literal: Ji Gong comforted and encouraged him, telling him to remain where he was for the night and move the next day.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Gong reassured him and let him stay where he was until the following day before relocating.

sentences.zh: 季恭到任，厘整浮華，翦罰遊惰，由是境內肅清。

translations.literal: When Ji Gong took office he rectified frivolity, punished idling and laxity, and thereby brought the territory to order.
translations.idiomatic: Once in office Ji Gong trimmed ostentation, punished loafers, and the district grew orderly and quiet.

sentences.zh: 累遷吳興太守，加冠軍。

translations.literal: He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wuxing, with the additional title Champion General.
translations.idiomatic: Further promotion made him Grand Administrator of Wuxing with the rank Champion General.

sentences.zh: 先是吳興頻喪太守，言項羽神為卞山王，居郡聽事，二千石常避之。

translations.literal: Before this Wuxing had repeatedly lost its grand administrators; it was said the spirit of Xiang Yu, as King of Bianshan, occupied the prefectural hall, and the two-thousand-dan officials regularly avoided it.
translations.idiomatic: Wuxing had a grim record of governors dying in office; locals said Xiang Yu's ghost, worshipped as the Bianshan King, haunted the audience hall, and incoming officials usually shunned it.

sentences.zh: 季恭居聽事，竟無害也。

translations.literal: Ji Gong sat in the audience hall and came to no harm.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Gong worked from that very hall and suffered no ill consequence.

sentences.zh: 遷尚書左僕射，固讓。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: Promoted to Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, he refused the appointment.

sentences.zh: 義熙八年，復為會稽內史，修飾學校，督課誦習。

translations.literal: In the eighth year of Yixi he again became Intendant of Kuaiji, repaired the schools, and supervised recitation and study.
translations.idiomatic: In Yixi 8 he returned as Kuaiji Intendant, restored the schools, and enforced the curriculum.

sentences.zh: 十年，復為右僕射，又讓不拜。

translations.literal: In the tenth year he was again made Right Vice Director but once more declined and did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: In year ten he was offered the Right Vice Directorship again and once more turned it down.

sentences.zh: 除領軍，加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: He was appointed Director of the Guard and given the additional post of Regular Attendant of the Privy.
translations.idiomatic: He was made Director of the Imperial Guard, with concurrent rank as Regular Attendant.

sentences.zh: 十二年致仕，拜金紫光祿大夫。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year he retired from office and was honored as Grand Master with the Purple-Gold Seal.
translations.idiomatic: In year twelve he retired and received the honorific title Grand Master of the Purple-Gold Seal.

sentences.zh: 是歲，武帝北伐，季恭求從，以為太尉軍諮祭酒。

translations.literal: That year, when Emperor Wu marched north, Ji Gong asked to follow and was made Libationer to the Army Staff of the Grand Commandant.
translations.idiomatic: The same year Liu Yu marched north; Ji Gong volunteered to join the campaign and was made army staff libationer under the Grand Commandant.

sentences.zh: 從平關、洛。

translations.literal: He followed in the pacification of Guan and Luo.
translations.idiomatic: He took part in the reconquest of the Guan region and Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 子靈符，位丹陽尹，會稽太守，尋加豫章王子尚撫軍長史。

translations.literal: His son Lingfu held the posts of Intendant of Danyang and Grand Administrator of Kuaiji, and was soon added as Chief Administrator to the Pacification Army of Prince Shang of Yuzhang.
translations.idiomatic: His son Lingfu served as Danyang Intendant and Kuaiji Grand Administrator, later becoming chief secretary to Prince Shang of Yuzhang's pacification staff.

sentences.zh: 靈符家本豐富，產業甚廣，又於永興立墅，周回三十三里，水陸地二百六十五頃，含帶二山，又有果園九處。

translations.literal: Lingfu's family was originally wealthy with vast holdings; he also established a manor at Yongxing spanning thirty-three li in circuit, with two hundred sixty-five qing of land by water and road, embracing two hills, and nine orchards besides.
translations.idiomatic: The Lingfu household was already rich with sprawling estates; at Yongxing he built a private manor thirty-three li around—two hundred sixty-five qing of land and waterways, two hills within the bounds, and nine orchards.

sentences.zh: 為有司所糾，詔原之。

translations.literal: He was impeached by the relevant offices and pardoned by imperial edict.
translations.idiomatic: Officials reported his excesses, but an edict let him off.

sentences.zh: 而靈符答對不實，坐免。

translations.literal: But Lingfu's answers in inquiry were untrue, and he was dismissed on that account.
translations.idiomatic: When questioned he lied under oath and was removed from office.

sentences.zh: 尋又復官。

translations.literal: Before long he was restored to office.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was reappointed.

sentences.zh: 靈符愨實有材幹，不存華飾，每所蒞官，政績修理。

translations.literal: Lingfu was earnest and capable, indifferent to ornament; wherever he served, governance was well ordered.
translations.idiomatic: Honest and capable, he cared nothing for display, and every post he held ran in good order.

sentences.zh: 廢帝景和中，犯忤近臣，為所讒構，遣使鞭殺之。

translations.literal: During the Jinghe era of the Deposed Emperor he offended a favorite close to the throne and was slandered by him; an envoy was sent to flog him to death.
translations.idiomatic: Under Deposed Emperor Liu Yu's Jinghe reign he crossed a court favorite and was framed; emissaries were sent to beat him to death.

sentences.zh: 二子湛之、深之於都賜死。

translations.literal: His two sons Zhanzhi and Shenzhi were granted death in the capital.
translations.idiomatic: His sons Zhanzhi and Shenzhi were ordered to take their own lives in the capital.

sentences.zh: 明帝即位，追贈靈符金紫光祿大夫。

translations.literal: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Lingfu was posthumously honored as Grand Master with the Purple-Gold Seal.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming posthumously ennobled Lingfu as Grand Master of the Purple-Gold Seal.

sentences.zh: 深之大明中為尚書比部郎。

translations.literal: Shenzhi served in the Daming era as Bureau Reviewer in the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: During the Daming reign Shenzhi was a Bureau Reviewer in the Ministry of Works.

sentences.zh: 時安陸應城縣人張江陵與妻吳共罵母黃令死，黃忿恨自經死，已值赦。

translations.literal: At the time Zhang Jiangling of Yingcheng County in Anlu and his wife Wu jointly reviled his mother Huang until she died; Huang died of resentment by hanging herself, and the case coincided with an amnesty.
translations.idiomatic: A case arose in Yingcheng, Anlu: Zhang Jiangling and his wife Wu abused his mother Huang until she hanged herself in despair—the crime fell under a general amnesty already proclaimed.

sentences.zh: 案律，子賊殺傷毆父母梟首，罵詈棄市，謀殺夫之父母亦棄市。

translations.literal: According to law, a son who kills, injures, or beats his parents is beheaded and displayed; reviling them brings execution in the market; plotting to murder a husband's parents also brings market execution.
translations.idiomatic: Statute held that sons who murder, wound, or beat parents suffer display of the severed head; verbal abuse warrants public execution, as does plotting against a husband's parents.

sentences.zh: 會赦，免刑補冶。

translations.literal: When an amnesty occurred, capital punishment was remitted and replaced with forced labor in the smelting works.
translations.idiomatic: Under amnesty, capital sentence became penal service at the imperial foundries.

sentences.zh: 江陵罵母，母以自裁，重於傷毆。

translations.literal: Jiangling reviled his mother and she killed herself—heavier than injury or beating.
translations.idiomatic: Jiangling's curses drove his mother to suicide—a worse offense than physical assault.

sentences.zh: 若同殺科則疑重，用傷毆及詈科則疑輕。

translations.literal: If treated under the homicide statute the penalty would seem too heavy; if under the injury-beating or reviling statutes, too light.
translations.idiomatic: Applied the murder statute and the penalty looked excessive; applied assault or abuse statutes and it looked too lenient.

sentences.zh: 制唯有打母遇赦猶梟首，無詈母致死會赦之科。

translations.literal: Regulations provided only that beating one's mother, even under amnesty, still brought display of the severed head; there was no provision for reviling a mother to death under amnesty.
translations.idiomatic: Only beating a mother remained a capital display offense even after amnesty; no clause covered verbal abuse that ended in a parent's suicide.

sentences.zh: 深之議曰：「夫題裏逆心而仁者不入，名且惡之，況乃人事？

translations.literal: Shenzhi argued: 'One whose heart harbors treachery against principle—benevolent men will not enter his village; even the name is loathsome, how much more the deed?
translations.idiomatic: Shenzhi submitted: 'Confucius said the benevolent do not dwell where disloyalty is advertised at the gate—if the very name is hateful, how much worse the act itself?

sentences.zh: 故毆傷咒詛，法所不原，詈之致盡，則理無可宥。

translations.literal: Thus beating and cursing are not forgiven by law; when reviling brings death, reason allows no pardon.
translations.idiomatic: Assault and malediction are never excused by law; abuse that ends in death admits no mercy in principle.

sentences.zh: 罰有從輕，蓋疑失善，求之文旨，非此之謂。

translations.literal: The principle that punishment may be lightened covers cases where guilt is doubtful or goodness has been lost; seeking the textual intent, this is not what is meant.
translations.idiomatic: Leniency applies when guilt is uncertain or mitigating virtue exists—nothing in the statutes supports leniency here.

sentences.zh: 江陵雖遇赦恩，故合梟首。

translations.literal: Though Jiangling encountered amnesty, he still should have his head displayed.
translations.idiomatic: Amnesty notwithstanding, Jiangling deserved the displayed head.

sentences.zh: 婦本以義，愛非天屬，黃之所恨，情不在吳，原死補冶，有允正法。

translations.literal: The wife was bound by marriage, not blood kin; Huang's grievance was not against Wu; remitting execution for penal labor accords with proper law.
translations.idiomatic: The wife owed duty by marriage, not blood—the mother bore no personal grudge against Wu; commuting her to foundry labor fit justice.

sentences.zh: 」詔如深之議，吳免棄市。

translations.literal: An edict followed Shenzhi's opinion; Wu was spared market execution.
translations.idiomatic: The throne accepted Shenzhi's reasoning and spared Wu from public execution.

sentences.zh: 靈符弟靈運位著作郎。

translations.literal: Lingfu's younger brother Lingyun held the post of Court Historian.
translations.idiomatic: Lingfu's brother Lingyun served as Court Historian.

sentences.zh: 靈運子琇之。

translations.literal: Lingyun's son Xianzhi.
translations.idiomatic: Lingyun was father to Xianzhi.

sentences.zh: 琇之有吏能，仕齊為吳令。

translations.literal: Xianzhi had administrative ability and served Qi as magistrate of Wu.
translations.idiomatic: Capable in administration, Xianzhi became magistrate of Wu under Qi.

sentences.zh: 有小兒年十歲，偷刈鄰家稻一束，琇之付獄案罪。

translations.literal: A boy of ten stole and cut a sheaf of his neighbor's rice; Xianzhi handed him to prison to be charged.
translations.idiomatic: When a ten-year-old stole a sheaf of a neighbor's rice, Xianzhi jailed him for trial.

sentences.zh: 或諫之，琇之曰：「十歲便能為盜，長大何所不為。

translations.literal: Someone admonished him; Xianzhi said, 'At ten he already steals—what will he not do when grown?
translations.idiomatic: Advisers protested. Xianzhi replied, 'A thief at ten will be anything at thirty.

sentences.zh: 」縣中皆震肅。

translations.literal: Throughout the county all were awed to order.
translations.idiomatic: The whole district fell silent and straight.

sentences.zh: 遷尚書左丞，又以職事知名。

translations.literal: He was promoted to Left Assistant Director of the Masters of Writing and became known for competence in office.
translations.idiomatic: Promotion to Left Assistant Director brought renown for flawless administration.

sentences.zh: 後兼左戶尚書，廷尉卿。

translations.literal: Later he concurrently served as Left Minister of the Household and as Court Commandant.
translations.idiomatic: He later doubled as Left Minister of the Household and Court Commandant.

sentences.zh: 出為臨海太守，在任清約。

translations.literal: Sent out as Grand Administrator of Linhai, he lived plainly and sparingly in office.
translations.idiomatic: As Linhai Grand Administrator he governed with austere simplicity.

sentences.zh: 罷郡還，獻幹薑二千斤，齊武帝嫌其少，及知琇之清，乃歎息。

translations.literal: When he left the commandery he offered two thousand jin of dried ginger; Emperor Wu of Qi thought it too little, but learning of Xianzhi's integrity, sighed in admiration.
translations.idiomatic: Leaving office he sent two thousand jin of dried ginger as tribute; Qi Emperor Wu at first scoffed at the amount, then sighed when he grasped Xianzhi's poverty.

sentences.zh: 出監吳興郡，尋拜太守，政稱清嚴。

translations.literal: He was sent to oversee Wuxing Commandery and soon appointed Grand Administrator; his governance was praised as clean and strict.
translations.idiomatic: Posted to supervise Wuxing and soon made its administrator, he earned a name for stern integrity.

sentences.zh: 子臻，至太子舍人，尚書三公郎。

translations.literal: His son Zhen rose to Attendant to the Heir Apparent and Gentleman in the Three Dukes section of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: His son Zhen became a crown prince attendant and a Secretariat officer in the Three Dukes bureau.

sentences.zh: 臻子幼孫，梁甯遠枝江公主簿、無錫令。

translations.literal: Zhen's son Yousun served as secretary to Princess Ningyuan of Zhijiang under Liang and as magistrate of Wuxi.
translations.idiomatic: Zhen's son Yousun was a Liang-era secretary to Princess Ningyuan of Zhijiang and magistrate of Wuxi.

sentences.zh: 幼孫子奐。

translations.literal: Yousun's son Huan.
translations.idiomatic: Yousun fathered Huan.

sentences.zh: 奐字休文，數歲而孤，為叔父虔孫所養，好學善屬文。

translations.literal: Huan, courtesy name Xiuwen, was orphaned young and raised by his uncle's son Qiansun; he loved learning and wrote well.
translations.idiomatic: Huan styled Xiuwen lost his parents in childhood and was raised by his cousin Qiansun; he was devoted to books and skilled at composition.

sentences.zh: 沛國劉顯以博學稱，每深相歎美，執其手曰：「昔伯喈墳素悉與仲宣，吾當希彼蔡君，足下無愧王氏。

translations.literal: Liu Xian of Pei was famed for erudition; he often sighed in deep admiration and clasped Huan's hand, saying, 'Long ago Cai Yong entrusted all his texts to Wang Can; I hope to be that Cai—you need not blush before the Wang clan.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xian of Pei, celebrated for learning, often grasped his hand in admiration: 'When Cai Yong gave his library to Wang Can, he knew a worthy heir—I mean to play Cai Yong; you would not disgrace the Wangs.

sentences.zh: 所保書籍，尋以相付。」

translations.literal: The books he keeps in trust will be handed to you before long.
translations.idiomatic: The volumes I guard will soon be yours.

sentences.zh: 仕梁為尚書儀曹侍郎。

translations.literal: He served Liang as Gentleman in the Ceremonial section of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: Under Liang he was a ceremonial officer in the Ministry of Rites.

sentences.zh: 時左戶郎沈炯為飛書所謗，將陷重辟，連官台閣，人懷憂懼，奐廷議理之，竟得明白。

translations.literal: At the time the Left Household Gentleman Shen Jiong was slandered by an anonymous letter and faced capital punishment; office after office was implicated and men lived in dread; Huan argued for him at court and he was finally cleared.
translations.idiomatic: Shen Jiong of the Left Household Bureau was nearly destroyed by an anonymous denunciation that threatened the whole Secretariat; Huan defended him in open debate until the case collapsed.

sentences.zh: 侯景陷建鄴，朝士並被拘縶，或薦奐于賊率侯子鑒，乃脫桎梏，厚遇之，令掌書記。

translations.literal: When Hou Jing took Jiankang, court officials were all detained; someone recommended Huan to the rebel leader Hou Zijian, who released him from bonds, treated him generously, and put him in charge of documents.
translations.idiomatic: After Hou Jing seized Jiankang the court elite were chained; a recommendation reached the rebel commander Hou Zijian, who freed Huan, favored him, and put him to writing dispatches.

sentences.zh: 時子鑒景之腹心，朝士莫不卑屈，奐獨無所下。

translations.literal: Zijian was Hou Jing's trusted lieutenant; court officials all bowed and cringed, but Huan alone would not defer.
translations.idiomatic: As Hou Jing's intimate, Zijian held every official groveling—Huan alone refused to bend.

sentences.zh: 或諫奐曰：「不宜高抗。

translations.literal: Someone counseled Huan: 'You should not stand so high and hard.
translations.idiomatic: A friend warned him: 'Do not provoke them from such a height.

sentences.zh: 」奐曰：「吾性命有在，豈有取媚凶醜，以求全乎。

translations.literal: Huan said, 'My life is still mine—how could I flatter vicious ugliness merely to survive?
translations.idiomatic: Huan answered, 'While I live by my own breath, I will not fawn on murderers to buy safety.

sentences.zh: 」時賊徒剝掠子女，拘逼士庶，奐保持得全者甚眾。

translations.literal: At the time the rebels plundered men and women and coerced gentry and commoners; many whom Huan sheltered were preserved whole.
translations.idiomatic: While bandits seized children and terrorized the city, Huan shielded a great many from harm.

sentences.zh: 尋遭母憂。

translations.literal: Before long he suffered mourning for his mother.
translations.idiomatic: Soon afterward his mother died.

sentences.zh: 時天下喪亂，皆不能終三年喪，唯奐及吳國張種在寇亂中，守法度，並以孝聞。

translations.literal: The realm was torn by chaos and mourning and none could complete the three-year rites; only Huan and Zhang Zhong of Wu, amid the disorder, kept the regulations and both were famed for filial piety.
translations.idiomatic: War had shattered the ritual calendar—almost no one completed a full mourning period—but Huan and Zhang Zhong of Wu kept the law amid chaos and won renown for filial devotion.

sentences.zh: 及景平，司徒王僧辯先下辟書，引為左西掾。

translations.literal: When Hou Jing was pacified, Minister of Education Wang Sengbian first issued a summons appointing him Left Western Aide.
translations.idiomatic: After Hou Jing's defeat Wang Sengbian, Minister of Education, summoned him as Left Western Aide.

sentences.zh: 梁元帝於荊州即位，征奐及沈炯，僧辯累表請留之。

translations.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang ascended at Jingzhou and summoned Huan and Shen Jiong; Sengbian repeatedly memorialized asking to retain them.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Yuan took the throne at Jingzhou he called Huan and Shen Jiong north; Sengbian memorialized again and again to keep them.

sentences.zh: 帝手敕報曰：「孔、沈二士，今且借公。

translations.literal: The emperor replied by personal rescript: 'The two gentlemen Kong and Shen I lend to you for now.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor answered in his own hand: 'Kong and Shen are yours on loan—for now.

sentences.zh: 」其為朝廷所重如此。

translations.literal: Such was the esteem in which the court held him.
translations.idiomatic: The court valued him to this degree.

sentences.zh: 僧辯為揚州刺史，又補中從事史。

translations.literal: When Sengbian became Governor of Yang Province, Huan was additionally appointed Attending Officer.
translations.idiomatic: When Sengbian took Yangzhou governorship, Huan was made his staff attending officer.

sentences.zh: 時侯景新平，每事草創，憲章故事，無復存者。

translations.literal: Hou Jing had only just been pacified; everything was newly improvised, and statutes and precedents no longer survived.
translations.idiomatic: With Hou Jing just defeated, the state had to be rebuilt from nothing—no protocols or precedents remained.

sentences.zh: 奐博物強識，甄明故實，問無不知，儀注體式，箋書表翰，皆出於奐。

translations.literal: Huan was broadly learned and strong in memory; he clarified ancient facts and knew all that was asked; ritual protocols and forms, memorials, letters, and official writing all came from Huan.
translations.idiomatic: Erudite and retentive, he could authenticate every antiquity; court ritual, memorial style, and diplomatic prose all passed through his hand.

sentences.zh: 陳武帝作相，除司徒左長史，遷給事黃門侍郎。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu of Chen served as Chancellor, Huan was appointed Left Chief of Staff to the Minister of Education and promoted to Supervising Censor in the Yellow Gate.
translations.idiomatic: When Chen Baxian became Chancellor, Huan was made the Education Minister's chief secretary, then Supervising Secretary in the Yellow Gate.

sentences.zh: 齊遣東方老、蕭軌來寇，四方壅隔，糧運不繼，三軍取給，唯在都下，乃除奐建康令。

translations.literal: Qi sent Dongfang Lao and Xiao Gui to raid; the four quarters were cut off and grain transport failed; the three armies drew supplies only from the capital region, so Huan was appointed magistrate of Jiankang.
translations.idiomatic: Qi dispatched Dongfang Lao and Xiao Gui to invade; supplies were severed nationwide and the army fed only from the capital—Huan was named magistrate of Jiankang.

sentences.zh: 武帝克日決戰，乃令奐多營麥飯，以荷葉裹之，一宿之間，得數萬裹。

translations.literal: The emperor set a day for decisive battle and ordered Huan to prepare great quantities of wheat meal wrapped in lotus leaves; within one night tens of thousands of bundles were made.
translations.idiomatic: On the eve of battle Chen Baxian ordered Huan to bake barley meal and wrap it in lotus leaves—by morning tens of thousands of rations stood ready.

sentences.zh: 軍人旦食訖，盡棄其餘，因而決戰，大破賊。

translations.literal: The soldiers ate in the morning and discarded the rest, then fought the decisive battle and routed the enemy.
translations.idiomatic: Men ate their fill at dawn, shed what remained, and charged to a crushing victory.

sentences.zh: 武帝受禪，遷太子中庶子。

translations.literal: When the emperor accepted the abdication, Huan was transferred to Palace Companion to the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: After Chen Baxian took the throne, Huan became a tutor in the crown prince's household.

sentences.zh: 永定三年，除晉陵太守。

translations.literal: In the third year of Yongding he was appointed Grand Administrator of Jinling.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongding 3 he became Grand Administrator of Jinling Commandery.

sentences.zh: 晉陵自宋、齊以來為大郡，雖經寇擾，猶為全實，前後二千石多行侵暴，奐清白自守，妻子並不之官，唯以單船臨郡。

translations.literal: Jinling Commandery had been a great prefecture since Song and Qi; though ravaged by bandits it remained intact and prosperous; successive grand administrators often practiced extortion; Huan kept himself pure—wife and children did not accompany him to office; he came to the commandery in a single boat alone.
translations.idiomatic: Jinling had been a major prefecture since Song and Qi; despite raids it stayed wealthy, and most governors preyed on it—Huan arrived alone in one small boat, family left home, pockets clean.

sentences.zh: 所得秩俸，隨即分贍孤寡，郡中號曰神君。

translations.literal: Salary and stipends he received were at once distributed to widows and orphans; the commandery called him the Divine Lord.
translations.idiomatic: He handed out every penny of salary to the destitute, and the district nicknamed him the Spirit-Magistrate.

sentences.zh: 曲阿富人殷綺見奐居處儉素，乃餉以衣氈一具。

translations.literal: Yin Qi, a wealthy man of Qu'a, saw Huan's dwelling was spare and plain and sent him a set of clothing and blankets.
translations.idiomatic: Yin Qi, a rich Qu'a merchant, saw how plainly Huan lived and sent a set of clothes and felt.

sentences.zh: 奐曰：「太守身居美祿，何為不能辦此？

translations.literal: Huan said, 'The Grand Administrator enjoys handsome stipend—why could he not provide this himself?
translations.idiomatic: Huan replied, 'A grand administrator on full salary ought to afford his own blankets—

sentences.zh: 但百姓未周，不容獨享溫飽。

translations.literal: But the people are not yet provided for—I cannot alone enjoy warmth and full bellies.
translations.idiomatic: —but my people still lack necessities; I cannot keep comfort while they go without.

sentences.zh: 勞卿厚意，幸勿為煩。」

translations.literal: Thank you for your generous intent; please do not trouble yourself further.
translations.idiomatic: I honor your kindness; please give yourself no further trouble.

sentences.zh: 遷散騎常侍，領步兵校尉、中書舍人。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Regular Attendant of the Privy, concurrently Commandant of Foot Soldiers and Palace Attendant of the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Promotion made him Privy Regular Attendant, with concurrent rank as infantry commandant and palace secretary.

sentences.zh: 重除御史中丞，尋為五兵尚書。

translations.literal: He was again appointed Censor-in-Chief and soon became Minister of the Five Armies.
translations.idiomatic: He was again made Censor-in-Chief, then Minister of War.

sentences.zh: 時文帝不豫，台閣眾事，並令僕射到仲舉共決。

translations.literal: Emperor Wen was unwell; all matters of the Secretariat were ordered decided jointly with Vice Director Dao Zhongju.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen fell ill, every Secretariat affair went to Vice Director Dao Zhongju for joint decision.

sentences.zh: 及帝疾篤，奐與宣帝及到仲舉並吏部尚書袁樞、中書舍人劉師知等入侍醫藥。

translations.literal: When the emperor's illness grew grave, Huan with Emperor Xuan, Dao Zhongju, Minister of Personnel Yuan Shu, and Palace Attendant Liu Shizhi and others entered to attend the medicine.
translations.idiomatic: As the illness worsened, Huan joined Emperor Xuan, Dao Zhongju, Minister of Personnel Yuan Shu, and Secretary Liu Shizhi at the sickbed.

sentences.zh: 文帝嘗謂奐等曰：「今三方鼎峙，宜須長君，朕欲近則晉成，遠隆殷法，卿等須遵此意。

translations.literal: Emperor Wen once told Huan and the others: 'Now three sides stand like tripods—we need a mature ruler; I wish to follow Jin's Emperor Cheng in the near view and exalt Yin precedent in the far; you must keep to this intent.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen once told them: 'Three kingdoms stand in balance—we need an experienced sovereign. I would have you emulate Jin's Cheng in near policy and the high Zhou in far ambition. Hold to that course.

sentences.zh: 」奐乃流涕歔欷跪而對曰：「陛下禦膳違和，痊復非久，皇太子春秋鼎盛，聖德日躋，廢立之事，臣不敢聞。

translations.literal: Huan wept and sobbed, knelt, and answered: 'Your Majesty's imperial repast is disordered—recovery is not far; the Crown Prince is in the prime of youth and his sage virtue rises daily; on deposition and installation I dare not hear.
translations.idiomatic: Huan wept and answered from his knees: 'Your Majesty's ailment is passing—the crown prince is young, strong, and daily growing in virtue. On removing an heir I must stay silent.

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「古之遺直，復見之卿。

translations.literal: The emperor said, 'The upright remnant of antiquity—I see him again in you.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, 'The stubborn integrity of the ancients lives again in you.

sentences.zh: 」乃用奐為太子詹事。

translations.literal: Thereupon Huan was appointed Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: Huan was then made Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.

sentences.zh: 廢帝即位，除散騎常侍、國子祭酒。

translations.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Huan was appointed Regular Attendant of the Privy and Grand Master of the Imperial Academy.
translations.idiomatic: Under the Deposed Emperor he became Privy Regular Attendant and Chancellor of the Imperial Academy.

sentences.zh: 出為南中郎康樂侯長史、尋陽太守，行江州事。

translations.literal: He was sent out as Chief Administrator to the Marquis of Kangle of the Southern Palace Attendant and Grand Administrator of Xunyang, acting in Jiang Province affairs.
translations.idiomatic: He was posted as chief secretary to the Marquis of Kangle, with concurrent duty as Xunyang Grand Administrator and acting governor of Jiang Province.

sentences.zh: 宣帝即位，為始興王長史。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, Huan became Chief Administrator to the Prince of Shixing.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan made him chief secretary to the Prince of Shixing.

sentences.zh: 奐在職清儉，多所規正，宣帝嘉之，賜米五百斛，並累降敕書，殷勤勞問。

translations.literal: In office Huan was pure and frugal and often offered corrective counsel; Emperor Xuan praised him, bestowing five hundred hu of grain and repeatedly sending edicts of warm inquiry.
translations.idiomatic: He governed with austere integrity and spoke plainly against error; Emperor Xuan rewarded him with five hundred hu of grain and a stream of affectionate rescripts.

sentences.zh: 太建六年，為吏部尚書。

translations.literal: In the sixth year of Taijian he became Minister of Personnel.
translations.idiomatic: In Taijian 6 he was appointed Minister of Personnel.

sentences.zh: 八年，加侍中。

translations.literal: In the eighth year he was given the additional post of Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Two years later he received concurrent rank as Palace Attendant.

sentences.zh: 時有事北邊，克復淮、泗，封賞敘用，紛紜重疊，奐應接引進，門無停賓。

translations.literal: At the time there were affairs on the northern frontier; Huai and Si were recovered, and enfeoffments and appointments piled up in confusion; Huan handled recommendations and promotions without a moment's pause at his gate.
translations.idiomatic: While the north was active and Huai-Si reconquest flooded the court with rewards and appointments, Huan's door never closed to petitioners seeking advancement.

sentences.zh: 加以識鑒人物，詳練百氏，凡所甄拔，衣冠搢紳莫不悅服。

translations.literal: Added to this was his discernment of men and mastery of many lineages; all whom he selected among the gentry and officials were pleased and convinced.
translations.idiomatic: His eye for talent and command of pedigree meant every man he elevated among officials and gentry accepted the choice without resentment.

sentences.zh: 性耿介，絕諸請托，雖儲副之尊，公侯之重，溺情相及，終不為屈。

translations.literal: By nature he was upright and severed all requests for favor; though the heir's dignity or the weight of dukes and marquises pressed him with personal feeling, he never yielded.
translations.idiomatic: Stubbornly upright, he refused every pull of patronage—even when crown princes or great lords pleaded on private grounds, he would not bend.

sentences.zh: 始興王叔陵之在湘州，累諷有司，固求台鉉。

translations.literal: When Prince Shixing's Shuling was in Xiang Province he repeatedly hinted to the relevant offices and stubbornly sought a post at the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Shixing's son Shuling, while governing Xiang Province, repeatedly leaned on officials to demand a capital appointment.

sentences.zh: 奐曰：「袞章本以德重，未必皇枝。

translations.literal: Huan said, 'The imperial regalia of office rests on weight of virtue—not necessarily on imperial descent.
translations.idiomatic: Huan replied, 'Grand seals belong to men of moral weight, not automatically to princes of the blood.

sentences.zh: 」因抗言于宣帝。

translations.literal: He therefore spoke boldly against this to Emperor Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: He spoke bluntly against the demand before Emperor Xuan.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「始興那忽望公，且朕兒為公，須在鄱陽王后。

translations.literal: The emperor said, 'How could Shixing harbor such hopes? And as my son he ranks after the Queen of Poyang.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, 'Shixing should not dream so high—and as my son he stands below the Queen of Poyang in precedence.

sentences.zh: 」奐曰：「臣之所見，亦如聖旨。

translations.literal: Huan said, 'What I see accords with Your Majesty's intent.
translations.idiomatic: Huan answered, 'My view matches Your Majesty's own.

sentences.zh: 」後主時在東宮，欲以江總為太子詹事，令管記陸瑜言之奐。

translations.literal: At the time the Later Lord was in the Eastern Palace and wished to make Jiang Zong Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent; he had his recorder Lu Yu speak to Huan about it.
translations.idiomatic: The future Later Lord, then crown prince, wanted Jiang Zong as Grand Tutor and sent his recorder Lu Yu to sound Huan out.

sentences.zh: 奐曰：「江有潘、陸之華，而無園、綺之實，輔弼儲貳，竊謂非材。

translations.literal: Huan said, 'Jiang has the brilliance of Pan and Lu but not the substance of Yuan and Qi; to assist the heir I privately deem him unfit.
translations.idiomatic: Huan said, 'Jiang has Pan Yue's polish and Lu Ji's glitter, not Yuan Ji's depth or Qi Wuhui's substance—he is no fit tutor for an heir.

sentences.zh: 」後主深以為恨，乃自言于宣帝。

translations.literal: The Later Lord deeply resented this and spoke of it himself to Emperor Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince nursed a deep grudge and complained directly to Emperor Xuan.

sentences.zh: 宣帝將許之，奐乃奏曰：「江總文華之人，今皇太子文華不少，無藉於總。

translations.literal: Emperor Xuan was about to consent; Huan then memorialized: 'Jiang Zong is a man of literary brilliance; the Crown Prince already has brilliance enough and has no need of Zong.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan nearly agreed until Huan memorialized: 'Jiang Zong is ornamental prose—the crown prince already has ornament enough without him.

sentences.zh: 如臣愚見，願選敦重之才，以居輔導。

translations.literal: In my humble view, I wish to select a man of solid weight to occupy the guiding post.
translations.idiomatic: I urge appointing a man of sober weight to guide the heir.

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「誰可？

translations.literal: The emperor said, 'Who would do?
translations.idiomatic: The emperor asked, 'Whom do you propose?

sentences.zh: 」奐曰：「都官尚書王廓，代有懿德，識性敦敏，可以居之。

translations.literal: Huan said, 'Wang Kuo, Minister of the Palace Bureau, comes from generations of fine virtue and is discerning and earnest—he can hold the post.
translations.idiomatic: Huan named Wang Kuo of the Palace Bureau—'a line of proven virtue, sharp and steady—he can hold the post.

sentences.zh: 」後主時亦在側，乃曰：「廓王泰之子，不可居太子詹事。

translations.literal: The Later Lord was also at the side and said, 'Kuo is Wang Tai's son—he cannot hold the Grand Tutorship to the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince, present at the audience, objected: 'Wang Kuo is Wang Tai's son—unsuitable for Grand Tutor.

sentences.zh: 」奐又曰：「宋朝范曄即範泰之子，亦為太子詹事。

translations.literal: Huan again said, 'In the Song dynasty Fan Ye, who was Fan Tai's son, also served as Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: Huan countered, 'Under Song, Fan Ye—Fan Tai's own son—served as Grand Tutor.

sentences.zh: 」後主固爭之，帝以總為詹事，由是忤旨。

translations.literal: The Later Lord stubbornly contested; the emperor made Zong Grand Tutor, and Huan thereby offended the imperial intent.
translations.idiomatic: The prince pressed his case; the emperor named Jiang Zong Grand Tutor anyway, and Huan fell from favor.

sentences.zh: 初，後主欲官其私寵，微諷於奐，奐不從。

translations.literal: Earlier the Later Lord had wished to give office to his private favorite and subtly hinted to Huan; Huan did not comply.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier the crown prince had tried to place a private favorite in office and hinted at Huan; Huan refused.

sentences.zh: 及左僕射陸繕遷職，宣帝欲用奐代繕，已草詔訖，後主抑遂不行。

translations.literal: When Left Vice Director Lu Shan was transferred, Emperor Xuan wished to use Huan in Shan's place; the draft edict was already written, but the Later Lord suppressed it and it was not carried out.
translations.idiomatic: When Left Vice Director Lu Shan moved on, Emperor Xuan drafted an edict naming Huan to replace him—the crown prince blocked it and the appointment never issued.

sentences.zh: 孔琳之字彥琳，會稽山陰人也。

translations.literal: Kong Linzhi, courtesy name Yanlin, was a native of Shanyin in Kuaiji.
translations.idiomatic: Kong Linzhi, styled Yanlin, came from Shanyin in Kuaiji.

sentences.zh: 曾祖群，晉御史中丞。

translations.literal: His great-grandfather Qun was Censor-in-Chief of Jin.
translations.idiomatic: His great-grandfather Qun had been Jin Censor-in-Chief.

sentences.zh: 祖沈，丞相掾。

translations.literal: His grandfather Shen was an aide to the Chancellor.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Shen served as a chancellor's aide.

sentences.zh: 父廞，光祿大夫。

translations.literal: His father Yin was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
translations.idiomatic: His father Yin held the title Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.

sentences.zh: 琳之強正有志力，少好文義，解音律，能彈棋，妙善草隸。

translations.literal: Linzhi was forceful and upright with firm resolve; in youth he loved literary principle, understood music, could play chess, and excelled at cursive and clerical script.
translations.idiomatic: Linzhi was stern, principled, and resolute; young he loved letters and ethics, knew music, played chess, and wrote superb cursive and clerical hand.

sentences.zh: 桓玄輔政為太尉，以為西合祭酒。

translations.literal: When Huan Xuan assisted in government as Grand Commandant, Linzhi was made Libationer of the Western Pavilion.
translations.idiomatic: While Huan Xuan governed as Grand Commandant, Linzhi was appointed Western Pavilion Libationer.

sentences.zh: 玄時議欲廢錢用穀帛，琳之議曰：

translations.literal: At the time Xuan debated abolishing coin and using grain and cloth instead; Linzhi argued:
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan then proposed abolishing coinage for grain and silk; Linzhi submitted:

sentences.zh: 洪範八政，以貨次食，豈不以交易之所資，為用之至要者乎。

translations.literal: The Hongfan's Eight Policies place wealth after food—surely because the medium of exchange is the essential resource of use.
translations.idiomatic: The Great Plan ranks wealth after grain precisely because currency is the lifeblood of exchange.

sentences.zh: 故聖王制無用之貨，以通有用之財，既無毀敗之費，又省難運之苦，此錢所以嗣功龜貝，歷代不廢者也。

translations.literal: Thus sage kings fashioned useless goods to circulate useful wealth, avoiding the cost of spoilage and the hardship of transport—this is why coin succeeded turtle shells and cowries and was never abandoned by successive ages.
translations.idiomatic: Sage kings invented token money to move real goods—no spoilage, no hauling—so coin replaced shells and cowries and every dynasty kept it.

sentences.zh: 穀帛為寶，本充衣食，今分以為貨，則致損甚多，又勞煩于商販之手，耗棄於割截之用，此之為弊，著於自曩。

translations.literal: Grain and cloth are treasures meant to clothe and feed; if divided to serve as currency, loss is great, and merchants' hands are troubled while cutting and trimming waste away—this harm has been evident since antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: Grain and cloth exist to feed and clothe; pressed into service as money they spoil in quantity, pass through too many merchant hands, and waste away in cutting and trimming—as every age has shown.

sentences.zh: 故鍾繇曰：「巧偽之人，競濕穀以要利，制薄絹以充資。

translations.literal: Thus Zhong Yao said: 'Crafty counterfeiters race to dampen grain for profit and weave thin silk to meet demand.
translations.idiomatic: Zhong Yao warned that fraudsters soak grain to cheat the scales and weave thin silk to pad accounts.

sentences.zh: 」魏世制以嚴刑，弗能禁也。

translations.literal: In Wei they imposed harsh punishments yet could not forbid it.
translations.idiomatic: Wei tried harsh law and still could not stop it.

sentences.zh: 是以司馬芝以為「用錢非徒豐國，亦所以省刑」。

translations.literal: Hence Sima Zhi held that 'using coin not only enriches the state but also reduces punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Zhi argued that coinage enriches the realm and cuts crime at the root.

sentences.zh: 今既用而廢之，則百姓頓亡其利，是有錢無糧之人，皆坐而饑困，此斷之之弊也。

translations.literal: Now to use it and then abolish it would suddenly strip the people of their gain—those with coin but no grain would sit and starve; this is the harm of cutting it off.
translations.idiomatic: Abolish coin now and the people lose their livelihood overnight—men holding cash but no grain will starve where they sit; that is the cost of prohibition.

sentences.zh: 魏明帝時，錢廢穀用四十年矣，以不便於人，乃舉朝大議，精才達政之士，莫不以為宜復用錢。

translations.literal: In Emperor Ming of Wei's time coin was abolished and grain used for forty years; because it inconvenienced the people, the whole court debated, and talented men versed in governance all held that coin should be restored.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Emperor Ming tried grain-only currency for forty years; when the burden on common life became unbearable, the court debated and every capable minister urged restoring coin.

sentences.zh: 彼尚舍穀帛而用錢，足以明穀帛之弊著於已試也。

translations.literal: They abandoned grain and cloth for coin—enough to show that the harm of grain and cloth was proven by trial.
translations.idiomatic: Their return to coin proved in practice what theory already showed: grain-money fails.

sentences.zh: 玄又議復肉刑，琳之以為：

translations.literal: Xuan also debated restoring corporal punishment; Linzhi held:
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan also proposed restoring mutilation punishments; Linzhi argued:

sentences.zh: 唐虞象刑，夏禹立辟，蓋淳薄既異，致化不同。

translations.literal: Tang and Yu used symbolic punishments; Xia Yu established capital statutes—because simplicity and harshness differed, their transforming influence differed.
translations.idiomatic: Tang and Yu relied on shame; Yu the Great codified death—cultures differ in purity and complexity, and so must their punishments.

sentences.zh: 書曰：「世輕世重」，言隨時也。

translations.literal: The Documents say 'light in one age, heavy in another'—meaning punishment follows the times.
translations.idiomatic: The Classic of Documents says penalties lighten or harden with the age—law must track its era.

sentences.zh: 夫三代風純而事簡，故罕蹈刑辟，季末俗巧而務殷，故動陷憲網。

translations.literal: The Three Dynasties had pure customs and simple affairs, so few touched the penal code; late ages were crafty and busy, so many fell into the net of law.
translations.idiomatic: When the Three Dynasties were simple, crime was rare; when late ages grew cunning and crowded, everyone tripped the statutes.

sentences.zh: 若三千行于叔世，必有踴貴之尤，此五帝不相循法，肉刑不可悉復者也。

translations.literal: If the three thousand statutes were applied in a decadent age, there would surely be cases of excessive severity—this is why the Five Emperors did not copy one another's laws, and corporal punishments cannot all be restored.
translations.idiomatic: Run the three-thousand statutes in a fallen age and cruelty will multiply—no sage emperor copied his predecessor's code wholesale, and mutilation cannot simply return.

sentences.zh: 漢文發仁惻之意，傷自新之路莫由，革古創制，號稱刑厝；

translations.literal: Emperor Wen of Han, moved by humane feeling, grieved that the path of reform had no outlet, and abolished the ancient forms, claiming to have set aside punishment;
translations.idiomatic: Han Emperor Wen, pitying the condemned, opened a path to renewal by abolishing ancient mutilations and proclaiming an end to harsh law;

sentences.zh: 然名輕而實重，反更傷人。

translations.literal: yet the name was light while the reality was heavy, and in the end more lives were harmed.
translations.idiomatic: yet the label softened while the blade did not—more men died for it.

sentences.zh: 故孝景嗣位，輕之以緩，緩而人慢，又不禁邪。

translations.literal: When Emperor Jing succeeded he lightened penalties to relax them; relaxation bred contempt and again failed to restrain evil.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Jing lightened sentences to soften the code; softness bred contempt and crime returned.

sentences.zh: 期於刑罰之中，所以見美於昔，歷代詳論而未獲厥中者也。

translations.literal: The aim was to find the mean within punishment—hence the praise of past ages—and generation after generation debated without finding the center.
translations.idiomatic: Every dynasty sought the golden mean in punishment and won praise when it neared—but none ever held the center long.

sentences.zh: 兵荒已後，罹法更多，棄市之刑，本斬右趾，漢文一謬，承而弗革，所以前賢悵恨，議之而未辯。

translations.literal: After the wars, those who violated law were more numerous; market execution originally meant cutting the right foot—Emperor Wen's one error was inherited and never corrected, which is why former sages lamented and debated without resolving it.
translations.idiomatic: After the wars, offenders multiplied. Market execution once meant cutting the right foot—Wen changed it once and successors never fixed the mistake; sages debated and still found no answer.

sentences.zh: 鍾繇、陳群之意雖小有不同，欲以右趾代棄市。

translations.literal: Zhong Yao and Chen Qun differed slightly in view but both wished to replace market execution with cutting the right foot.
translations.idiomatic: Zhong Yao and Chen Qun disagreed in detail but both would trade public beheading for amputation of the right foot.

sentences.zh: 若從其言，則所活者眾矣。

translations.literal: If their counsel had been followed, those who lived would have been many.
translations.idiomatic: Had their counsel prevailed, countless lives would have been spared.

sentences.zh: 降死之生，誠為輕法，可以全其性命，蕃其產育，仁既濟物，功亦益眾。

translations.literal: Commuting death to life is indeed a lighter law; it can preserve life and increase offspring; benevolence aids the people and the merit multiplies.
translations.idiomatic: Replacing death with mutilation is gentler law—it preserves life and families multiply; mercy spreads and the benefit compounds.

sentences.zh: 又今之所患，逋逃為先，屢叛不革，宜令逃身靡所，亦以肅戒未犯，永絕惡原。

translations.literal: Again, today's trouble puts fugitives first; repeated rebellion goes uncorrected—fugitives should have nowhere to hide, both to warn those not yet guilty and to cut off the root of evil forever.
translations.idiomatic: Today's plague is flight from justice—repeat rebels escape reform. Make fugitives nowhere welcome: warn the innocent and dry up rebellion at the source.

sentences.zh: 至於餘條，宜且依舊。

translations.literal: As for the remaining articles, they should for now follow the old.
translations.idiomatic: Other statutes may remain as they stand for now.

sentences.zh: 玄好人附悅，而琳之不能順旨，是以不見知。

translations.literal: Xuan loved men who flattered and pleased him, and Linzhi could not bend to his intent; therefore he was not recognized.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan favored sycophants; Linzhi would not trim his views to please—and went unrewarded.

sentences.zh: 累遷尚書左丞，揚州中從事史，所居著績。

translations.literal: He rose through posts to Left Assistant Director of the Masters of Writing and Attending Officer of Yang Province, achieving distinction wherever he served.
translations.idiomatic: He climbed to Left Assistant Director and Yangzhou Attending Officer, leaving a record of achievement at every post.

sentences.zh: 時責眾官獻便宜，議者以為宜修庠序，恤典刑，審官方，明黜陟，舉逸拔才，務農簡調。

translations.literal: At the time all officials were ordered to submit practical proposals; debaters held that schools should be restored, canonical punishments tended, official posts examined, promotions and demotions clarified, hidden talent raised, and agriculture favored while levies simplified.
translations.idiomatic: The court solicited practical reforms: restore schools, enforce canonical law, audit offices, clarify promotion, elevate hidden talent, favor farmers, lighten taxes.

sentences.zh: 琳之於眾議之外，別建言曰：

translations.literal: Beyond the common proposals Linzhi separately submitted:
translations.idiomatic: Apart from the common memorials Linzhi offered two further proposals:

sentences.zh: 夫璽印者，所以辨章官爵，立契符信。

translations.literal: Seals and stamps exist to distinguish ranks and offices and establish contractual trust.
translations.idiomatic: Seals exist to mark rank and bind trust between offices.

sentences.zh: 官莫大于皇帝，爵莫尊于公侯，而傳國之璽，歷代遞用，襲封之印，弈世相傳。

translations.literal: No office is greater than the emperor's, no nobility higher than duke or marquis—yet the seal of dynastic transmission passes through ages, and the seal of hereditary enfeoffment passes from generation to generation.
translations.idiomatic: No rank exceeds the emperor's, no title outranks duke or marquis—yet the dynastic seal passes unchanged through reigns and hereditary seals from father to son.

sentences.zh: 貴在仍舊，無取改作。

translations.literal: What matters is continuity—there is no call to remake them.
translations.idiomatic: Continuity is the point—there is no need to recast them.

sentences.zh: 今世唯尉一職獨用一印，至於內外群官，每遷悉改，討尋其義，私所未達。

translations.literal: Today only the Commandant of the Guard uses one seal per office; for all other inner and outer officials, each transfer brings a new seal—I have examined the rationale and cannot grasp it privately.
translations.idiomatic: Today only the guard commandant keeps one seal per tenure; every other official gets a fresh seal at every transfer—I cannot see the sense in it.

sentences.zh: 若謂官各異姓，與傳襲不同，則未若異代之為殊也；

translations.literal: If one says each office bears a different surname unlike hereditary transmission, then different dynasties are even more unlike one another;
translations.idiomatic: If the argument is that offices differ by surname unlike hereditary titles, then changing dynasties differs even more radically;

sentences.zh: 若論其名器，雖有公卿之貴，未若帝王之重；

translations.literal: if one speaks of name and vessel, though there is the honor of duke or minister, it does not match the weight of emperor;
translations.idiomatic: if the argument is rank and regalia, even a duke's dignity cannot match an emperor's;

sentences.zh: 若以或有誅夷之臣，忌其凶穢，則漢用秦璽，廷祚四百，未聞以子嬰身戮國亡而棄不佩。

translations.literal: if one fears executed ministers and shuns their ill omen, Han used Qin's seal and the dynasty lasted four hundred years—I have never heard that because Ziying was slain and the state perished the seal was cast aside and not worn.
translations.idiomatic: if the fear is ill luck from executed ministers, Han wore Qin's seal for four hundred years—no one discarded it because Ziying died and Qin fell.

sentences.zh: 帝王公侯之尊，不疑於傳璽，人臣眾僚之卑，何嫌于即印？

translations.literal: Emperors and nobles need not doubt the transmission seal; why should humble officials scruple at using the seal of their immediate office?
translations.idiomatic: Thrones and duchies trust inherited seals without scruple—why should a clerk flinch at the seal on his desk?

sentences.zh: 載籍未聞其說，推例自乖其准，而終年刻鑄，喪功消實，金銀銅炭之費，不可稱言，非所以因循舊貫，易簡之道。

translations.literal: Records nowhere mention this doctrine; by analogy it contradicts its own standard—yet year after year casting wastes labor and substance, and the cost in gold, silver, copper, and charcoal cannot be reckoned; this is not the way to follow old practice and simplify.
translations.idiomatic: No classic supports the custom; precedent argues against it—yet the court casts new seals every year, burning gold, silver, copper, and charcoal beyond counting. That is not continuity; it is waste.

sentences.zh: 愚請眾官即用一印，無煩改作，若新置官，又官多印少，文或零失，然後乃鑄，則仰裨天府，非唯小益。

translations.literal: I humbly ask that all officials use one seal without repeated recasting; only when a new office is created and seals are too few, or documents are lost, should new ones be cast—then the imperial treasury gains, not merely a small benefit.
translations.idiomatic: Let every official keep one seal through his tenure; cast anew only for new posts or lost documents—the treasury saves more than a little.

sentences.zh: 又曰：

translations.literal: He also said:
translations.idiomatic: He further wrote:

sentences.zh: 凶門柏裝，不出禮典，起自末代，積習生常，遂成舊俗，爰自天子達于庶人。

translations.literal: The mourning gate hung with cypress is not in the ritual canon; it arose in late ages, hardened by habit into custom, reaching from Son of Heaven down to commoners.
translations.idiomatic: Cypress-draped mourning gates appear nowhere in the classics—they are a late habit grown into custom from emperor to commoner.

sentences.zh: 誠行之有由，卒革必駭；

translations.literal: If practice has its reasons, sudden abolition would surely shock;
translations.idiomatic: Custom has momentum; sudden abolition would alarm;

sentences.zh: 然苟無關於情，而有愆禮度，存之未有所明，去之未有所失，固當式遵先典，厘革後謬，況復兼以游費，實為人患者乎。

translations.literal: yet if it bears no relation to feeling yet violates ritual measure, keeping it clarifies nothing and removing it loses nothing—we should follow the ancient canon and correct later error, especially when combined with wasteful display it truly harms the people.
translations.idiomatic: yet where feeling is untouched and ritual violated, keeping the custom explains nothing and dropping it costs nothing—follow the ancients, cut the later mistake, especially this drain on common purses.

sentences.zh: 凡人士喪儀，多出閭里，每有此須，動十數萬，損人財力，而義無所取。

translations.literal: Funeral rites of gentlemen mostly come from village custom; whenever this is needed, tens of thousands are spent, wasting men's wealth and strength for rites that gain nothing.
translations.idiomatic: Gentry funerals follow village fashion; each one burns tens of thousands in wealth and labor for ceremony that buys nothing.

sentences.zh: 至於寒庶，則人思自竭，雖復室如懸罄，莫不傾產單財，所謂「葬之以禮」，其若此乎？

translations.literal: Among the poor, men still exhaust themselves; though their houses hang empty they pour out every asset—this is what 'bury with ritual' has come to mean?
translations.idiomatic: Even the poor bankrupt themselves—houses bare, fortunes gone—is this what 'burial by ritual' was meant to be?

sentences.zh: 謂宜一罷凶門之式。

translations.literal: I hold that the mourning-gate form should be abolished entirely.
translations.idiomatic: Abolish the cypress mourning gate entirely.

sentences.zh: 遷尚書吏部郎。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Gentleman in the Personnel section of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: He was moved to a personnel officer in the Ministry of Works.

sentences.zh: 義熙十一年，除宋武帝平北、征西長史，遷侍中。

translations.literal: In the eleventh year of Yixi he was appointed Chief of Staff to the Pacifying North and Pacifying West armies and promoted to Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: In Yixi 11 he became chief of staff to the northern and western pacification armies and was promoted to Palace Attendant.

sentences.zh: 宋台初建，除宋國侍中。

translations.literal: When the Song regime was first established he was appointed Palace Attendant of the State of Song.
translations.idiomatic: When the Song state was founded he became Song Palace Attendant.

sentences.zh: 永初二年，為御史中丞，明憲直法，無所屈橈，奏劾尚書令徐羨之虧違憲典。

translations.literal: In the second year of Yongchu he became Censor-in-Chief, clarifying statutes and upholding law without bending; he impeached the Director of the Masters of Writing Xu Xianzhi for violating the constitutional canon.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongchu 2 he became Censor-in-Chief, enforcing law without fear, and impeached Director Xu Xianzhi for breaching constitutional order.

sentences.zh: 時羨之領揚州刺史，琳之弟璩之為中從事，羨之使璩之解釋琳之，使停寢其事。

translations.literal: At the time Xianzhi also held the governorship of Yang Province; Linzhi's younger brother Qunzhi was Attending Officer, and Xianzhi had Qunzhi intercede with Linzhi to halt the case.
translations.idiomatic: Xianzhi also governed Yangzhou; Linzhi's brother Qunzhi served on his staff, and Xianzhi sent Qunzhi to persuade Linzhi to drop the impeachment.

sentences.zh: 琳之不許，曰：「我觸忤宰相，政當罪止一身。

translations.literal: Linzhi would not agree, saying, 'I have offended the Chancellor—punishment should stop at me alone.
translations.idiomatic: Linzhi refused: 'I crossed the Chancellor—let punishment fall on me alone.

sentences.zh: 汝必不應從坐，何須勤勤邪。

translations.literal: You certainly should not be implicated—why such earnest pleading?
translations.idiomatic: You need not share my guilt—why beg so hard?

sentences.zh: 」自是百僚震肅，莫敢犯禁。

translations.literal: From then on the hundred officials were awed to order and none dared violate prohibition.
translations.idiomatic: After that the bureaucracy trembled and no one dared break the law.

sentences.zh: 武帝甚嘉之，行經蘭台，親加臨幸。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu greatly praised him; passing the Censorate he personally visited.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu admired him greatly and paid a personal visit when passing the Censorate.

sentences.zh: 遷祠部尚書，不事產業，家尤貧素。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Minister of Sacrifices, did not pursue estates, and his household was especially poor and plain.
translations.idiomatic: Made Minister of Sacrifices, he ignored property; his household stayed famously austere.

sentences.zh: 景平元年卒，追贈太常。

translations.literal: In the first year of Jingping he died; posthumously he was honored as Minister of Ceremonies.
translations.idiomatic: He died in Jingping 1 and was posthumously ennobled Minister of Ceremonies.

sentences.zh: 子邈有父風，官至揚州中從事。

translations.literal: His son Miao had his father's manner and rose to Attending Officer of Yang Province.
translations.idiomatic: His son Miao inherited his father's character and became Yangzhou Attending Officer.

sentences.zh: 邈子覬。

translations.literal: Miao's son Xi.
translations.idiomatic: Miao was father to Xi.

sentences.zh: 覬字思遠，少骨鯁有風力，以是非為己任。

translations.literal: Xi, courtesy name Siyuan, was from youth stern and forceful, taking right and wrong as his own charge.
translations.idiomatic: Xi styled Siyuan was blunt and forceful from youth, making moral judgment his personal duty.

sentences.zh: 口吃，好讀書，早知名。

translations.literal: He stuttered, loved reading, and was early known.
translations.idiomatic: He stuttered, read constantly, and was famous early.

sentences.zh: 歷位中書黃門侍郎。

translations.literal: He held successive posts including Gentleman in the Yellow Gate of the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He served through posts up to Secretariat Gentleman in the Yellow Gate.

sentences.zh: 初，晉安帝時，散騎常侍選望甚重，與侍中不異，其後職任閒散，用人漸輕。

translations.literal: At first, in Emperor An's time, Regular Attendant of the Privy was a selection of great weight, no different from Palace Attendant; afterward the duty grew idle and appointments gradually lighter.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor An, Privy Regular Attendant ranked with Palace Attendant; later the post hollowed out and appointments grew trivial.

sentences.zh: 孝建三年，孝武欲重其選，於是吏部尚書顏竣奏以覬及司徒左長史王景文應舉。

translations.literal: In the third year of Xiaojian, Emperor Xiaowu wished to restore weight to the selection and had Minister of Personnel Yan Jun memorialize that Xi and Wang Jingwen, Left Chief of Staff to the Minister of Education, should be nominated.
translations.idiomatic: In Xiaojian 3 Emperor Xiaowu tried to restore the post's prestige and had Minister of Personnel Yan Jun nominate Xi and Education Minister's chief secretary Wang Jingwen.

sentences.zh: 帝不欲威權在下，其後分吏部尚書置二人以輕其任。

translations.literal: The emperor did not wish authority to rest below; afterward he split the Ministry of Personnel into two ministers to lighten the burden.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor would not let power sit below him; he then split the Ministry of Personnel in two to dilute its weight.

sentences.zh: 侍中蔡興宗謂人曰：「選曹要重，常侍閑淡，改之以名而不以實，雖主意欲為輕重，人心豈可變邪？

translations.literal: Palace Attendant Cai Xingzong told others: 'The Personnel Bureau is essential and weighty; Regular Attendant is idle and thin—changing the name without changing the substance, though the sovereign's intent was to shift weight, can men's hearts be altered?
translations.idiomatic: Cai Xingzong remarked, 'Personnel is vital; Privy Attendant is ornamental—you rename without reweighting; the throne may intend a shift, but will men feel it?

sentences.zh: 」既而常侍之選復卑，選部之貴不異。

translations.literal: Before long the selection for Regular Attendant again sank low, and the Personnel Bureau's honor was unchanged.
translations.idiomatic: Soon Privy Attendant sank again while the Personnel Bureau kept its prestige.

sentences.zh: 大明元年，徙太子中庶子，領翊軍校尉，曆秘書監，廷尉卿，為御史中丞。

translations.literal: In the first year of Daming he was transferred to Palace Companion to the Heir Apparent, concurrently Commandant of the Guarding Army, and successively served as Director of the Secretariat, Court Commandant, and Censor-in-Chief.
translations.idiomatic: In Daming 1 he became crown prince companion and Guarding Army Commandant, then Secretariat Director, Court Commandant, and Censor-in-Chief in turn.

sentences.zh: 鞭令史，為有司所糾，原不問。

translations.literal: He flogged a clerk and was impeached by the relevant offices but pardoned without inquiry.
translations.idiomatic: He beat a clerk, drew an official complaint, and was let off without investigation.

sentences.zh: 六年，除安陸王子綏後軍長史、江夏內史。

translations.literal: In the sixth year he was appointed Chief Administrator to Prince Zisui of Anlu's Rear Army and Intendant of Jiangxia.
translations.idiomatic: In year six he became rear-army chief secretary to Prince Zisui of Anlu and Intendant of Jiangxia.

sentences.zh: 性使酒仗氣，每醉輒彌日不醒，僚類間多所陵忽，尤不能曲意權幸，莫不畏而疾之。

translations.literal: By nature he was given to wine and swagger; when drunk he often remained unconscious for whole days, and among colleagues he often looked down on many; he especially could not bend to the will of the powerful and favored—all feared and resented him.
translations.idiomatic: He drank hard and swaggered; drunk he slept for days, bullied colleagues, and refused to court the powerful—men feared and hated him.

sentences.zh: 居常貧罄，無有豐約，未嘗關懷。

translations.literal: In daily life he was constantly poor and empty, without abundance or scarcity, and never troubled himself over it.
translations.idiomatic: He lived in perpetual poverty and never cared whether times were lean or flush.

sentences.zh: 為府長史，典簽諮事，不呼前不敢前，不令去不敢去。

translations.literal: As chief of staff to the prince's household, the registry clerks consulted on affairs—without being summoned they dared not advance, without being dismissed they dared not leave.
translations.idiomatic: As princely chief of staff he terrified his registry clerks—they would not step forward unbidden or leave without orders.

sentences.zh: 雖醉日居多，而明曉政事，醒時判決，未嘗有壅。

translations.literal: Though drunk most days, he understood governance clearly; when sober his judgments were never blocked.
translations.idiomatic: Drunk most days yet lucid in office—sober, his rulings never stalled.

sentences.zh: 眾咸曰：「孔公一月二十九日醉，勝世人二十九日醒也。

translations.literal: All said: 'Master Kong is drunk twenty-nine days of the month and still outdoes the world awake twenty-nine days.
translations.idiomatic: Men joked, 'Kong is drunk twenty-nine days a month and still beats the rest of us awake twenty-nine days.

sentences.zh: 」孝武每欲引見，先遣人覘其醉醒。

translations.literal: Emperor Xiaowu whenever he wished to summon him first sent someone to observe whether he was drunk or sober.
translations.idiomatic: Before every audience Emperor Xiaowu sent scouts to learn whether Xi was drunk or sober.

sentences.zh: 性真素，不尚矯飾，遇得寶玩，服用不疑，而他物粗敗，終不改易。

translations.literal: By nature he was plain and genuine, not given to pretense; when he obtained treasures or curios he used them without hesitation, while other things though coarse and worn he never replaced.
translations.idiomatic: Plain and unpretending, he used fine gifts without fuss and wore threadbare things without replacing them.

sentences.zh: 時吳郡顧覬之亦尚儉素，衣裘器服皆擇其陋者。

translations.literal: At the time Gu Yan of Wu Commandery also valued frugality; fur coats and utensils he chose the shabbiest.
translations.idiomatic: Gu Yan of Wu Commandery was also famed for thrift—he picked the shabbiest furs and furnishings.

sentences.zh: 宋世清儉，稱此二人。

translations.literal: Under Song, purity and frugality—these two men were named.
translations.idiomatic: Song's age of austere virtue was spoken of through these two men.

sentences.zh: 覬弟道存、從弟徽，頗營產業，二弟請假東還，覬出渚迎之，輜重十餘船，皆是綿絹紙席之屬。

translations.literal: Xi's younger brother Daocun and his cousin cousin Hui both pursued estates; the two brothers asked leave to return east, and Xi went to the islet to meet them—more than ten boats of baggage, all silk, paper, and mats.
translations.idiomatic: Xi's brother Daocun and cousin Hui traded in property; returning east they met Xi at the river with a dozen boats loaded with silk, paper, and mats.

sentences.zh: 覬見之偽喜，謂曰：「我比乏，得此甚要。

translations.literal: Xi saw this and feigned delight, saying, 'I have been short lately—getting this is very needful.
translations.idiomatic: Xi pretended delight: 'I have been hard up—this cargo is welcome.

sentences.zh: 」因命置岸側，既而正色謂曰：「汝輩忝預士流，何至還東作賈客邪？

translations.literal: He ordered it placed on the shore, then with stern face said, 'You share in the rank of gentlemen—how can you return east to play merchant?
translations.idiomatic: He had it unloaded, then said coldly, 'You hold gentry rank—why come east like peddlers?

sentences.zh: 」命燒盡乃去。

translations.literal: He ordered it all burned and then left.
translations.idiomatic: He ordered the whole convoy burned and walked away.

sentences.zh: 先是，庾徽之為御史中丞，性豪麗，服玩甚華，覬代之，衣冠器用莫不粗率。

translations.literal: Before this Yu Hui had been Censor-in-Chief, by nature lavish, with splendid dress and playthings; Xi replaced him and official garb and utensils were all coarse.
translations.idiomatic: His predecessor Yu Hui had been a lavish Censor-in-Chief draped in finery; Xi replaced him in rough clothes and plain gear.

sentences.zh: 蘭台令史並三吳富人，咸有輕之之意。

translations.literal: The Censorate clerks and wealthy men of the Three Wu all held him in contempt.
translations.idiomatic: Censorate clerks and Three Wu magnates looked down on him.

sentences.zh: 覬蓬首緩帶，風貌清嚴，皆重跡屏氣，莫敢欺犯。

translations.literal: Xi with unkempt hair and loose belt, bearing stern and clear, all stepped lightly and held their breath, none daring to offend.
translations.idiomatic: Unkempt hair, loose sash, gaze like ice—clerks and magnates held their breath and dared not test him.

sentences.zh: 庾徽之字景猷，潁川鄢陵人也，後卒于南東海太守。

translations.literal: Yu Hui, courtesy name Jingyou, was a native of Yanling in Yingchuan; he later died as Grand Administrator of Southern Donghai.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Hui styled Jingyou came from Yanling in Yingchuan and later died as Southern Donghai Grand Administrator.

sentences.zh: 覬後為司徒左長史，道存代覬為後軍長史、江夏內史。

translations.literal: Xi later became Left Chief of Staff to the Minister of Education; Daocun replaced Xi as Rear Army Chief Administrator and Intendant of Jiangxia.
translations.idiomatic: Xi later served as Education Minister's chief secretary; Daocun took his old post as rear-army chief and Jiangxia Intendant.

sentences.zh: 時東土大旱，都邑米貴，一斗將百錢。

translations.literal: At the time the eastern lands suffered great drought; in the capital grain was dear—a dou nearly a hundred cash.
translations.idiomatic: The east was in severe drought; capital grain hit nearly a hundred cash per dou.

sentences.zh: 道存慮覬甚乏，遣吏載五百斛米餉之。

translations.literal: Daocun worried Xi was very destitute and sent an official to carry five hundred hu of grain as gift.
translations.idiomatic: Daocun, fearing Xi's poverty, sent an officer with five hundred hu of grain.

sentences.zh: 覬呼吏謂之曰：「我在彼三載，去官之日，不辦有路糧。

translations.literal: Xi summoned the officer and said, 'I was there three years; on the day I left office I could not even prepare travel rations.
translations.idiomatic: Xi called the officer in: 'Three years in that post and I left without travel money.

sentences.zh: 郎至彼未幾，那能得此米邪？

translations.literal: You have not been there long—how could you obtain this grain?
translations.idiomatic: You have barely arrived—where did this grain come from?

sentences.zh: 可載米還彼。

translations.literal: Carry the grain back there.
translations.idiomatic: Take it back upstream.

sentences.zh: 」吏曰：「自古以來無有載米上水者，都下米貴，乞於此貨之。

translations.literal: The officer said, 'Since antiquity there has never been grain carried upstream; grain is dear in the capital—I beg to sell it here.
translations.idiomatic: The officer protested, 'No one hauls grain upstream; capital prices are high—let us sell here.

sentences.zh: 」不聽，吏乃載米而去。

translations.literal: Xi would not listen; the officer then carried the grain away.
translations.idiomatic: Xi refused; the officer sailed the grain away.

sentences.zh: 庾業既東，明帝即以代延熙為義興，以延熙為巴陵王休若鎮東長史。

translations.literal: After Yu Ye had gone east, Emperor Ming at once replaced Yan Xi with him as Grand Administrator of Yixing, and made Yan Xi Chief Administrator to Prince Xiuruo of Baling's Eastern Pacification staff.
translations.idiomatic: Once Yu Ye marched east, Emperor Ming swapped Yan Xi for Ye as Yixing Grand Administrator and made Yan Xi chief secretary to Prince Xiuruo of Baling's eastern command.

sentences.zh: 業至長塘湖，即與延熙合。

translations.literal: Ye reached Changtang Lake and at once joined Yan Xi.
translations.idiomatic: Ye reached Changtang Lake and joined Yan Xi immediately.

sentences.zh: 明帝遣建威將軍沈懷明東討，尚書張永系進。

translations.literal: Emperor Ming sent the General Who Establishes Might Shen Huaiming east to suppress them; the Master of Writing Zhang Yong advanced in support.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming sent General Shen Huaiming east against them with Master of Writing Zhang Yong in support.

sentences.zh: 巴陵王休若董統東討諸軍。

translations.literal: Prince Xiuruo of Baling directed all eastern suppression armies.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Xiuruo of Baling commanded the eastern suppression forces.

sentences.zh: 時覬所遣孫曇瓘等軍頓晉陵九里，部陣甚盛。

translations.literal: At the time the army Xi had sent under Sun Tanqian halted at Jiuli in Jinling; their formation was very grand.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Tanqian's division—sent by Xi—camped at Jiuli in Jinling in imposing array.

sentences.zh: 懷明至奔牛，所領寡弱，張永至曲阿，未知懷明安否，退還延陵就休若。

translations.literal: Huaiming reached Benniu with weak forces; Zhang Yong reached Qu'a, not knowing whether Huaiming was safe, and retreated to Yanling to join Prince Xiuruo.
translations.idiomatic: Huaiming reached Benniu undermanned; Zhang Yong, reaching Qu'a without news of him, fell back to Yanling to Prince Xiuruo.

sentences.zh: 諸將帥咸勸退破岡，休若宣令敢有言退者斬，眾小定。

translations.literal: All generals urged retreat to Pogang; Prince Xiuruo proclaimed that whoever spoke of retreat would be beheaded, and the ranks steadied.
translations.idiomatic: Generals urged retreat to Pogang; Prince Xiuruo decreed death for anyone who spoke of retreat, and the army steadied.

sentences.zh: 軍主劉亮又繼至，兵力轉集，人情乃安。

translations.literal: Army commander Liu Liang arrived next, forces gathered further, and men's hearts settled.
translations.idiomatic: Commander Liu Liang arrived with reinforcements and morale settled.

sentences.zh: 時齊高帝率軍東討，與張永等於晉陵九里曲結營，與東軍相持。

translations.literal: At the time Emperor Gao of Qi led armies east to suppress them; with Zhang Yong and others at Jiuli in Jinling he pitched linked camps and faced the eastern army.
translations.idiomatic: Qi Emperor Gao marched east and with Zhang Yong linked camps at Jiuli in Jinling, facing the rebel east.

sentences.zh: 上遣積射將軍江方興、南台御史王道隆至晉陵視賊形勢，賊帥孫曇瓘、程扞宗、陳景遠凡有五城，互相連帶。

translations.literal: The throne sent the General of Accumulated Shots Jiang Fangxing and the Southern Terrace Censor Wang Daolong to Jinling to observe the enemy; the rebel commanders Sun Tanqian, Cheng Hanzong, and Chen Jingyuan held five walled positions in mutual support.
translations.idiomatic: The court sent General Jiang Fangxing and Censor Wang Daolong to scout Jinling; rebel leaders Sun Tanqian, Cheng Hanzong, and Chen Jingyuan held five linked fortresses.

sentences.zh: 扞宗城猶未固，道隆率所領急攻之，俄頃城陷，斬扞宗首。

translations.literal: Hanzong's wall was not yet firm; Daolong led his force in urgent attack and in a moment the city fell; Hanzong's head was cut off.
translations.idiomatic: Hanzong's wall was still weak; Daolong stormed it, the fort fell in moments, and Hanzong was beheaded.

sentences.zh: 劉亮果勁，便刀楯，乃負楯而進，直入重柵，眾軍因之，即皆摧破。

translations.literal: Liu Liang was truly fierce; taking blade and shield he bore the shield and advanced, plunging straight into the inner palisade; the mass of armies followed and all were shattered.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Liang fought like a demon—shield on arm he smashed the inner palisade and the whole army poured through.

sentences.zh: 齊高帝與永等乘勝馳擊之，又大破之。

translations.literal: Emperor Gao of Qi with Yong and the others pursued in victory and again routed them greatly.
translations.idiomatic: Qi Emperor Gao and Zhang Yong chased the rout and broke them again.

sentences.zh: 曇瓘因此敗走，孔璪與曇生焚倉庫，奔錢唐。

translations.literal: Tanqian therefore fled in defeat; Kong Zuan with Tansheng burned the storehouses and fled to Qiantang.
translations.idiomatic: Tanqian fled; Kong Zuan and Tansheng torched the granaries and ran for Qiantang.

sentences.zh: 會稽聞西軍稍近，將士多奔亡，覬不能復製。

translations.literal: Kuaiji heard the western army drawing near; officers and soldiers mostly fled, and Xi could no longer control them.
translations.idiomatic: As imperial forces neared Kuaiji, troops deserted in droves and Xi lost control.

sentences.zh: 上虞令王晏起兵攻郡，覬憂遽不知所為。

translations.literal: The magistrate of Shangyu, Wang Yan, raised troops to attack the commandery; Xi in panic knew not what to do.
translations.idiomatic: Shangyu magistrate Wang Yan raised troops against the prefecture; Xi panicked.

sentences.zh: 其夕率千人聲雲東討，實趨石賜。

translations.literal: That evening he led a thousand men, proclaiming an eastern campaign, but in fact hurried to Shici.
translations.idiomatic: That night he led a thousand men, claiming an eastern expedition, but fled toward Shici.

sentences.zh: 遇潮涸不得去，眾叛都盡，門生載以小船，竄於山脊村。

translations.literal: The tide ebbed and he could not leave; the masses all rebelled and departed; a student loaded him in a small boat and hid on a mountain ridge village.
translations.idiomatic: The tide went out and trapped him; his force melted away; a student rowed him in a skiff to a mountain hamlet.

sentences.zh: 村人縛以送晏，晏調曰：「此事孔璪所為，無豫卿事，可作首辭，當相為申上。

translations.literal: Villagers bound him and sent him to Yan; Yan jested, 'This was Kong Zuan's doing—you had no part; you may compose the chief confession and I will plead for you above.
translations.idiomatic: Villagers bound him for Wang Yan, who said lightly, 'Kong Zuan did this, not you—write the lead confession and I will speak for you at court.

sentences.zh: 」覬曰：「江東處分，莫不由身，委罪求活，便是君輩行意耳。

translations.literal: Xi said, 'Dispositions east of the river all proceed from oneself—to shift guilt and seek life is your kind's way.
translations.idiomatic: Xi answered, 'Every decision east of the Yang was mine—shift blame to live? That is your trade, not mine.

sentences.zh: 」晏乃斬之東合外。

translations.literal: Yan then beheaded him outside the eastern pavilion.
translations.idiomatic: Yan beheaded him outside the eastern hall.

sentences.zh: 臨死求酒，曰：「此是平生所好。

translations.literal: Facing death he asked for wine, saying, 'This was my lifelong delight.
translations.idiomatic: At the block he asked for wine: 'This was my lifelong pleasure.

sentences.zh: 」顧琛、王曇生、袁標等並詣吳喜歸罪，喜皆宥之。

translations.literal: Gu Chen, Wang Tansheng, Yuan Biao and others all went to Wu Xi to surrender and accept punishment; Xi pardoned them all.
translations.idiomatic: Gu Chen, Wang Tansheng, Yuan Biao, and others surrendered to Wu Xi for judgment; he pardoned them all.

sentences.zh: 東軍主凡七十六人，於陣斬十七人，餘皆原宥。

translations.literal: Eastern army commanders numbered seventy-six in all; seventeen were beheaded in battle, the rest pardoned.
translations.idiomatic: Seventy-six eastern commanders in all—seventeen killed in battle, the rest spared.

sentences.zh: 覬之起兵也，夢行宣陽門道上，顧望皆丘陵。

translations.literal: When Xi raised troops he dreamed of walking on the Xuanyang Gate road; looking back, all was hills and mounds.
translations.idiomatic: When Xi rebelled he dreamed of walking the Xuanyang Gate road and seeing only hills behind him.

sentences.zh: 覬寤，私告人曰：「丘陵者弗平，建康其殆難克。」

translations.literal: Xi awoke and privately told others, 'Hills and mounds mean not level—Jiankang will hardly be taken.
translations.idiomatic: He woke and whispered, 'Hills mean no level ground—Jiankang will not fall easily.

sentences.zh: 覬弟道存，位黃門吏部郎、南郡太守。

translations.literal: Xi's younger brother Daocun held the posts of Gentleman in the Yellow Gate Personnel section and Grand Administrator of Nan Commandery.
